Student Mentorship & Advising

Additionally, I supported them through the graduate school application process by reviewing their resumes, CVs, and portfolios, and helping them build personal websites.
I have also collaborated on the conceptualization and design of graduate research projects, as well as data analysis aimed at publication in peer-reviewed journals.

1. Professional and academic services

I have provided extensive professional and academic service to sustain the scholarly community and advance institutional missions, including conducting peer reviews for scientific journals and mentoring, training, and advising emerging researchers and students. Several of these initiatives were carried out through Ecodiversa Tropical, a Colombian NGO dedicated to biodiversity conservation.


TrainingPeer reviewMentorshipWebinars



Training junior scientists and conservation practitioners
I am committed to creating opportunities for early-career scientists and practitioners to build skills in data analysis and modeling for conservation. To that end, Prof. Melissa Guzmán (Cornell University) and I developed a series of Spanish-language R tutorials (see GitHub repo) designed to train Colombian undergraduate and graduate students alongside conservation practitioners. We also successfully raised funds to help bridge the conservation genetics knowledge gap across the Spanish-speaking Global South (see Experiment initiative).
Here is a look at the workshops we have developed so far:

Al final de este taller motivacional usted podrá responder a:

title: Education
text:
My academic background and research integrate wildlife field ecology, landscape spatial analysis, and macroecological patterns of biodiversity to advance conservation from local to global scales. This work is grounded in extensive field experience across terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems, alongside advanced training in spatial analysis and predictive modeling.







PhD. in Biology, University of Ottawa, Ottawa, Canada. (2018)





Research topic: Predicting broad-scale patterns of species endemism and conservation priorities.
Supervisor: Dr. Jeremy Kerr
My doctoral research synthesized large-scale global datasets to model the ecological and evolutionary drivers of species endemism. By applying rigorous validation tests to standard macroecological hypotheses, I demonstrated that current broad-scale models fall short of explaining global endemism patterns, highlighting essential directions for future macroecological research. Additionally, I evaluated the global protected area network’s historical growth relative to Aichi Target 11 benchmarks, designing targeted spatial priorities to extend protection to more than 1,500 unprotected endemic vertebrate species.
Publications:

Zuloaga, J., D. Currie & J. Kerr. (2019). The origins and maintenance of global species endemism. Global Ecology and Biogeography. 28(2): 170-183.
Zuloaga, J. and Kerr, J. T. (2017), Over the top: do thermal barriers along elevation gradients limit biotic similarity? Ecography, 40: 478–486. doi:10.1111/ecog.01764.
Boucher-Lalonde, V., R. De Camargo, J.M. Fortin, S. Khair S., R. So, Watson, D., Vasquez, H., Zuloaga, J., Currie, D. (2015). The weakness of the evidence supporting tropical niche conservatism as a main driver of current richness–temperature gradients. Global Ecology and Biogeography, 24(7):795-803.
Leroux, S., M. Larrivee, V. Boucher-Lalonde, A. Hurford, J. Zuloaga, J. T. Kerr, and F. Lutscher (2013). Mechanistic models for the spatial spread of species under climate change. Ecological Applications, 23(4), 815-828










Master in Environmental Studies (MES), York University, Toronto Canada. (2011)





Research topic: Identifying suitable sites for multiple focal species using an ecological niche factor analysis in Toronto and Region.
Supervisor: Dr. Gail Fraser & Dr. Howard Daugherty.
I used spatial distribution models and Ecological Land Classification (ELC) to predict high suitability areas for multiple focal species in Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA) jurisdiction. My results were used to provide science-based advice to planning managers for habitat restoration purposes within the TRCA’s Natural Heritage System (see here).









Certificate in Applied Digital Geography & GIS. Ryerson University, Toronto, Canada. (2008).





I mastered digital geography principles and concepts, fundamnetal GIS skills and applications (ArcGIS products), and data interpretation and analytical skills. See certificate here.









Bachelor of Science in Biology, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Bogotá, Colombia (1995).





Research topic: Densidad de población, hábitos alimenticios y anotaciones sobre hábitat natural del jaguar (Panthera onca L.) en la depresión inundable del bajo San Jorge.
In the floodplains of the Bajo San Jorge (northern Colombia), population density was estimated at 1–2 individuals per 150 km², with reptiles constituting the primary diet.
The most critical jaguar habitat in the region is the zapales, a dense mix of water-tolerant (hygrophytic) shrubs and trees and vegetation shaped by seasonal flood dynamics, especially in the rainy season. During the dry season, jaguars shift their spatial habitat use toward ciénagas (open-water marshes). This seasonal expansion escalates conflicts with local ranchers due to perceived and actual cattle losses.
Accomplishments:
Based on my experience and knowledge of jaguars in Colombia, I was invited as a contributing expert by the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) to join an international team of researchers focused on prioritizing the Americas’ jaguar conservation program. In this role, I compiled and validated all known jaguar occurrence records across Colombia. Through a series of collaborative workshops, our team synthesized continental datasets to identify and prioritize key Jaguar Conservation Units (JCUs) across major habitat types throughout the species’ entire geographic range.
Contribution:

Sanderson, E.W., K.H. Redford, C.B. Chetkiewicz, R.A. Medellin, A.R. Rabinowitz, J.G. Robinson, A.B. Taber. 2002. Planning to Save a Species: The Jaguar as a Model. Conservation Biology, 16(1): 58-72.

title: Work experiences
text:
My professional experience spans leadership, field ecology, spatial analysis, and applied research. As a project manager, I have led interdisciplinary teams, engaged diverse stakeholders, and overseen sustainable development and conservation initiatives from planning through execution and evaluation. My background also includes extensive fieldwork establishing flora and fauna baselines and evaluating environmental impacts, as well as roles as a spatial analyst and institutional researcher developing workflows, coding and decision-support tools to evaluate predictive models and guide local, national and global conservation efforts.







Statistical Ecologist - Alberta Biodiversity Monitoring Institute. Calgary, Canada (2025-2026).





The Alberta Biodiversity Monitoring Institute (ABMI) is a provincial leader in biodiversity monitoring and a nationally recognized model for government agencies and research institutions across Canada. Through broad collaboration, the ABMI provides timely, relevant, and scientifically credible data on Alberta’s living resources to support informed decision-making.
My role:
I worked as a Statistical Ecologist at the ABMI, responsible for creating tools to support environmental management in Alberta, and all across Canada. I leveraged R software and tools to develop interactive web applications, incorporating spatial data to deliver meaningful insights. Using GitHub for version control, I systematically tracked project progress and ensured clean code collaboration. Beyond technical development, I dedicated substantial time to technical writing—authoring comprehensive user guidelines and a publication-ready manuscript. Additionally, I co-organized and facilitated workshops focused on model evaluation tools to empower users and foster collaborative learning.
Accomplishments:

I co-developed sdmEvaluationTool, an interactive R Shiny application designed to help users evaluate the reliability, utility, and potential risks of species distribution models (SDMs) in conservation decision-making. The tool enables stakeholders to assess model performance before applying findings to real-world management strategies. Currently, beta testing is underway to refine the user experience and ensure robust performance.
I co-developed a decision-support tool that allows stakeholders to identify and prioritize key evaluation criteria for SDMs based on their specific biodiversity conservation and management objectives. To support wider adoption and methodology transparency, I am currently co-authoring a manuscript detailing the framework for model evaluation criteria.










Research Associate, McGill University. Montreal, Canada (2021- 2025).





Supervisor: Dr. Andrew Gonzalez

1. Bon in a Box (GEO BON)2. Models and Tools (Parks Canada)


Partners: GEO BON, Microsoft, Canada (McGill University, Université de Sherbrooke, Université Concordia and Université de Montréal) and Colombia (Humboldt Institute).
BON in a Box is an open-source, collaborative platform developed by the Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network (GEO BON) to help scientists, conservationists, and policymakers monitor biodiversity and report on global goals. This infrastructure empowers nations to effectively monitor biodiversity change and make data-driven conservation decisions. What is in the Box?

My role:
As a Research Associate at McGill University, I developed end-to-end spatial data workflows and engineered automated R pipelines to calculate Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) and ecological indicators. In addition to executing complex spatial analyses, I synthesized extensive peer-reviewed literature, authored technical user guidelines, and co-authored a research manuscript to showcasing the BON in a box collaborative platform.
Accomplishments:

I developed automated pipelines for ecological modeling. For technical details and source code, explore the BON in a Box GitHub Repository
Collaborated to develop the Spatio Temporal Asset Catalog (STAC, see STAC Viewer GEO BON) to support the implementation of EBVs and biodiversity indicators. STAC Catalog GitHub Repository.

Publications:
Griffith, J., …. J. Zuloaga, et al. BON in a Box:An Open and Collaborative Platform for Biodiversity Monitoring, Indicator Calculation, and Reporting
Click on this figure to access the STAC catalog (a collection of environmental layers):







Partner: Parks Canada
This work contributes to a Parks Canada initiative that collaborates with diverse partners to build the foundational knowledge required for conservation across the Hudson–James Bay Lowlands (HJBL). The initiative focuses on protecting the region’s exceptional biodiversity alongside its critical carbon stocks and fluxes across wetland, peatland, and coastal ecosystems. The HJBL plays a vital role in global climate regulation while providing essential ecosystem services—such as water retention and regulation, wild foods, and biocultural practices—that sustain the livelihoods and cultural heritage of local Indigenous communities.
My role:
I synthesized extensive peer-reviewed literature, grey literature, and web platforms to evaluate models, tools, and frameworks for monitoring biodiversity, ecosystem services, and scenario assessments. To communicate these findings effectively, I authored a comprehensive final report, developed an interactive R Shiny summary dashboard, and convened an expert workshop with leading practitioners in the field to foster collaborative insights.
Accomplishments:

I led the development of a HJBL toolbox incorporating ecological models, analytical tools, and standardized approaches to measure, monitor, and evaluate biodiversity and ecosystem services. Tailored specifically to the Hudson-James Bay Lowlands (HJBL) and broader northern ecosystems in Canada, this framework provides essential decision-support for regional conservation and environmental monitoring.
I developed a Summary for decision makers here.





















Postdoctoral Researcher, McGill University. Montreal, Canada (2019-2021)





Supervisor: Dr. Andrew Gonzalez

1. Key Biodiversity AreasThe Nature Conservancy


Partner: Wildlife Conservation Society (Co-supervisors: Ciara Raudsepp-Hearne and Justina Ray)
The Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) Initiative is a worldwide conservation planning tool aimed to identify potential sites that might contribute significantly to the global persistence of biodiversity (IUCN 2016).  It was designed to include multiple facets of biodiversity, spanning from species to communities and ecosystems. The KBA guidelines (IUCN 2016) suggest five high-level strategic criteria for its implementation: Threatened Biodiversity (A), Geographically Restricted Biodiversity (B), Ecological Integrity (C), Biological Processes (D), and Irreplaceability (E). Since 2017, more than 16,000 sites have been identified globally (KBA dashboard, visited in November 2024) and 188 in Canada (KBA Canada dashboard, visited in November 2024), mostly under criteria A, B and D.
My role:
I developed automated R pipelines and spatial analysis workflows to identify potential Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) across Canada for species that might trigger criteria A and B (threatened and geographically restricted species, respectively). Additionally, I led the development of a novel methodological approach to operationalize the Ecological Integrity criterion—prioritizing expansive landscapes with low industrial footprints and thriving biological communities to ensure robust, scalable application within national and global conservation frameworks.

1.1. Habitat Suitability Models
Accomplishments:

I developed a pipeline to implement habitat suitability models (HSMs, see some results here.) to help identify potential areas for Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) in Canada. See GitHub repository for pipeline. We ran the pipelines for a group of 96 species, that might trigger some KBA’s criteria, as a proof of concept aimed to provide recommendations for a full implementation (~ 1,200 species). The figure below shows the metodological framework for implementing HSMs.








1.2. Implementing the Ecological Integrity (EI) criterion
Accomplishments:

I led a national scoping analysis that integrated comprehensive global and national data sets on human pressures and biotic intactness across Canada’s terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems. Through this work, I identified Candidate Areas of Low Human Pressure and characterized their underlying biotic intactness, establishing a data-driven foundation for ongoing conservation planning and prioritization. (manuscript in progress).

Figure 1. General scoping analysis approach to implement the EI in Canada. In Step1 we identify Candidate Areas of Low Human Pressure (CA-LHPs) in Canada by subtracting from the national human footprint dataset for Canada  (HFP-Can by Hirsh-Pearson et al. 2022) a compilation of multiple global, national and provincial and territorial datasets from  a) terrestrial realm (human footprint, roads, seismic lines, etc.), and b) freshwater realm (Connectivity Status Index for rivers (CSI) within HYDRObasins). c) We tested multiple assumptions (e.g., effect of multiple HFP-Can thresholds, multiple buffers to rasterize vector datasets and minimum size of continuous area of low human pressure). d) We also compared our results with global and provincial datasets. In Step 2: Characterized the BI of these CA-LPHs.




Partner: The Nature Conservancy of Canada

2.1. Habitat Suitability Models
My role:
I collaborated directly with NCC to adapt the technical framework and pipelines built for the KBAs to meet their specific regional conservation priorities and land management objectives.
Accomplishments:
Building on our work with Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs), Nature Conservancy Canada (NCC) engaged our team to customize and implement our automated R pipelines and spatial workflows. See GitHub scripts here.













GIS Specialist, World Wildlife Fund. Toronto, Canada (2011)





Supervisors: James Snider and Steven Price
Free-flowing Rivers is an initiative of World Wildlife Fund-Canada (WWF-Canada) to ensure Canada’s wild rivers remain wild for the wildlife and people who depend on them.
My role:
I conducted spatial and network analyses to estimate the status of environmental rivers flows in Canada.
I collected, cleaned, and properly organized the HydroSHEDS hydrography data set for Canada, including quality control, node layers creation and stream order attribution to the network). Then, I applied spatial (e.g., ArcGIS: model Builder and Python) and network analyses (RivEx – a network processing tool) to evaluate the impact of various infrastructure features on rivers in Canada and to estimate the status of environmental flows and forecast likely future conditions of rivers network in Canada.
Accomplishments:

Generated multi-scale maps illustrating the status of free-flowing rivers across Canada, ranging from sub-basin to basin levels.
Developed reproducible spatial workflows to calculate river connectivity status, designed for easy replication and updating as new data becomes available.
Built a centralized geodatabase to store analytical results, enabling end-users to query, consult, and customize the outputs.

Publications:
My work and results was used to create this report:
Crochetiere et al. (2017). Wild and free-flowing: Identifying and safeguarding Canada’s wild rivers. WWF-Canada. 38p.

Project Coordinator. Universidad Nacional de Colombia (1998-2000).






Wildlife conservation portafolioStrategies for protecting non-forest ecosystems


The Ministry of Environment developed a strategy to access World Bank funding for the protection and management of wildlife in Colombia. To this end, the National University of Colombia (Universidad Nacional) was commissioned to build a project portfolio addressing the needs not only of academia, such as scientific research, but also of NGOs, local communities, indigenous communities, and various productive sectors, with the goal of protecting and sustainably managing fauna across all regions of Colombia.
My role:

Program Development: Spearheaded a wildlife conservation project portfolio, establishing standardized application procedures, proposal templates, and comprehensive guidelines to assist NGOs and universities in securing funding for fauna management.
Stakeholder Outreach & Engagement: Led regional outreach initiatives, delivering over 30 presentations to universities, non-profits, and research institutions to drive high-quality proposal submissions for wildlife protection and management.

Accomplishments:

Technical Evaluation & Portfolio Management: Evaluated and categorized 400+ project proposals based on maturity and developmental stage, streamlining the review and selection pipeline for conservation grants.



The Ministry of Environment planned to define conservation strategies for non-forest ecosystems in Colombia, including savannas, páramos, arid zones, and wetlands. To support this effort, the National University of Colombia (Universidad Nacional) was commissioned to synthesize baseline knowledge on each ecosystem’s spatial extent, physical determinants (geology and hydrography), flora and fauna, major threats, socioeconomic stressors, human impacts, and local and Indigenous populations, alongside recommendations for sustainable management and economic activities.
My role:

Coordinated an interdisciplinary team.
Developed a comprehensive literature review.
Organized a database, including multiple aspects for each ecosystems.

Accomplishments:

Synthesized baseline data and formulated sustainable management strategies to protect critical non-forest ecosystems in Colombia, including savannas, páramos, arid zones, and wetlands.

GeoIngeniería Ltda. (now part of Antea Group) is a multidisciplinary engineering and environmental consultancy that provides specialized technical, scientific, and regulatory expertise, guiding public and private sector clients in minimizing environmental risk and ensuring sustainable outcomes across complex infrastructure and resource projects.
My role and accomplishments:

End-to-End Project Management: Managed project life cycles from proposal design and budgeting to cost control, work plan execution, and site supervision, delivering high-quality documents on time and within scope.

Team Building & Quality Management: Recruited and mentored junior scientists in biological survey methodologies and environmental assessment frameworks; implemented ISO 9000 quality management standards to standardize workflow procedures.

Designed and delivered course modules examining Colombia’s major biogeographic regions and ecosystems. Emphasis on macroecological patterns and biophysical drivers (e.g., climate seasonality, geomorphology, and hydrologic regimes) controlling ecosystem boundaries from high-altitude Páramos to lowland rainforests.

title: Field experiences
text:
Driven by a deep curiosity for all forms of life, my fieldwork spans a wide range of ecosystems—from lowland tropical rainforests, savannas, and arid zones to high-Andean páramos and cloud forests, as well as wetlands, river systems, and coastal marine environments. My field experience includes research on jaguar ecology and multi-taxa surveys of mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles, and insects (particularly wild bees), alongside plant phenology and hydrobiological studies. Across these projects, I have applied standardized monitoring protocols, including transects, point counts, live trapping, camera trapping, bird banding, and sea turtle nesting surveys, to establish baselines for species richness, abundance, and habitat use.







Monitoring sea turtles. York University & COTERC. Tortuguero, Costa Rica (2010)





I served as a field assistant for the sea turtle monitoring program at the Caño Palma Biological Station (COTERC) in Tortuguero, Costa Rica.

Conducted nocturnal beach patrols to monitor and safeguard nesting leatherback and hawksbill sea turtles.
Recorded clutch sizes, collected biometric measurements, and applied identity tags to support long-term population tracking and conservation management.cal diversity across local, regional, and global scales.
Executed daily morning beach surveys to monitor sea turtle nest emergence and evaluate hatching success.
Documented post-hatching metrics, including shell counts and emerging hatchlings, to evaluate nest productivity and mortality rates.



Monitoring sea turtles in Tortuguero, Costa Rica












Bird banding, Costa Rica Bird Observatories (2010)





Invited by ornithologist Pablo Elizondo, I assisted with bird-banding operations across several key field sites in Costa Rica, including Tortuguero, Las Cruces Biological Station (Estación Biológica Las Cruces), and La Selva Biological Station (Estación Biológica La Selva).














Bird banding, Tommy Thompson Park Research Station, Toronto, Canada (2009-2011)





Over multiple field seasons, I have contributed to the avian monitoring program at the Tommy Thompson Park Bird Research Station, supporting standardized field surveys and long-term data collection to track migratory and resident bird populations.
















Implementing camera-traps. Las Nubes, Costa Rica (2009)





I initiated a camera-trapping program to identify terrestrial fauna at the Las Nubes Reserve.





Exiting news! Camera-trap footage of a tigrillo captured during fauna monitoring surveys in Las Nubes Reserve.

Terrestrial monitoring, Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA), Canada (2007-2010)





I contributed to the Terrestrial Monitoring Program at the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority (TRCA) in Toronto, supporting standardized ecological field surveys across urban and peri-urban natural areas. This work involved collecting long-term vegetation and wildlife data to track ecosystem health, assess habitat integrity, and inform regional watershed conservation and land management decisions









Field biologist. GeoIngeniería Ltda. (1995-2001)





I led interdisciplinary teams in collecting baseline data on terrestrial and freshwater flora and fauna to support more than 40 Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs) across diverse regions of Colombia, spanning tropical rainforests in the Amazon, mountain ecosystems in the Andes, savannas in the Orinoquía, and arid and semi-arid inter-Andean valleys.

Terrestrial Flora & Vegetation Assessments: Designed and executed standardized botanical inventories and forest structure assessments to characterize habitat composition, identify endemic or threatened plant species, and map ecological sensitivity across operational footprints.
Terrestrial Fauna & Biodiversity Surveys: Conducted multi-taxa wildlife monitoring, encompassing birds, mammals, amphibians, and reptiles, using standardized sampling protocols (e.g., transects, point counts, and trapping) to establish species richness, abundance, and habitat use baselines.
Hydrobiological & Aquatic Ecosystem Monitoring: Led freshwater sampling campaigns evaluating macroinvertebrates, ichthyofauna, periphyton, and plankton communities alongside physicochemical water quality parameters to assess aquatic ecosystem health and baseline biotic integrity.
Ecological Baseline & Vulnerability Modeling: Integrated multi-season terrestrial and aquatic field datasets to establish pre-intervention ecological baselines, evaluate habitat vulnerability to operational stressors, and inform targeted mitigation and conservation management plans.










Colombian ecosystems - Universidad Nacional de Colombia





Throughout my early scientific training in Colombia, I gained broad, multidisciplinary field and laboratory experience across diverse ecosystems, from high-Andean páramos and cloud forests to Amazonian river basins, and across multiple taxonomic groups, including mammals, insects, birds, reptiles, and plants.

High-Andean Ecosystem Ecology: Conducted field ecological research in páramo and upper Andean forest (bosque altoandino) ecosystems with the High Andean Ecosystems Studies Lab (Prof. Luis Eduardo Mora-Osejo):

Plant Phenology: Conducted field phenological monitoring in páramo ecosystems, documenting floration and fructification cycles across multiple native plant species to evaluate seasonal reproductive patterns and environmental drivers.
Restoration Planting Design: Designed site-specific planting and revegetation strategies, selecting resilient native flora from páramo and bosque altoandino, and optimizing establishment protocols to accelerate ecological succession and ecosystem recovery.

Mastozoology Lab (Prof. Alberto Cadena):

Particitapted in systematic collections of neotropical mammals in multiple locations.
Formulated the Feline Conservation Program in Colombia.

OIKOS Ecological Studies Group: Carried out field ecological studies and biodiversity assessments in the Sierra de la Macarena National Natural Park (Parque Nacional Natural Sierra de la Macarena), a major biogeographic transition zone connecting the Andes, Amazon, and Orinoquía.
Bee Lab (Prof. Guiomar Nates): I conducted extensive field collections and identification of native wild bees across multiple regions of Colombia, sampling diverse taxa including bumblebees (Bombus), large carpenter bees (Xylocopa), and stingless bees (Meliponini) to support taxonomic and ecological research.
Freshwater & Riverine Ecology: Contributed to the Ecology of Colombian Rivers project with the Limnology Lab (Profs. Gabriel Guillot and Germán Márquez), executing hydrobiological field surveys for the ecological characterization of the Putumayo River in the Colombian Amazon.
Colombian National Herbarium (Herbario Nacional Colombiano): Served as a curator, managing botanical specimens, verifying taxonomic identifications, and supporting floristic documentation.

title: Juan Zuloaga, PhD.
text:
Juan Zuloaga, PhD.


Biodiversity Conservation Scientist


I am a biodiversity conservation scientist who turns complex ecological data into practical solutions for nature and people.


Working across sectors, I lead interdisciplinary teams to design, implement, and evaluate strategies that protect wildlife, restore natural habitats, foster sustainable local livelihoods, and advance national and global biodiversity targets.
